CGU1iqBpiBQ.title: The Values of Islam: Mas'uliyyah and Istikhlaf (Responsibility and Stewardship)
CGU1iqBpiBQ.one_line: Humans are stewards, not owners: with unique power comes answerability for oneself, family, community, creatures and the earth, and the opposite is indifference.
CGU1iqBpiBQ.summary: The sheikh pairs responsibility, which looks both back and forward, with stewardship, a forward-looking care that depends on it. Moral maturity, which we demand of children, means seeing what we hold as entrusted rather than owned, and adults forget to apply it to their homes, families and jobs. Humanity's place in the ecosystem is unique: unlike animals that adapt, humans reshape their environment, so power brings obligation and answerability, whether for climate change or for artificial intelligence, which needs stewards more than more intelligence. He grounds this in Allah appointing a khalifah on earth, Ibrahim made an imam, nations made successors to be tested, and the hadith that each of us is a shepherd who will be questioned. The hadith of planting a sapling as the Hour arrives shows that one does one's part however small. Responsibility starts with oneself but does not end there: Abu Bakr corrected those misusing the verse about minding oneself, and the ship parable shows we sail or sink together. Responsibility then widens with ability, from self to family, business and community. Its opposite is indifference. Dawud, who held nearly every human role, was the Quran's model khalifah, and Umar feared being asked about a stumbling animal. Children must be raised as caregivers.

outline.heading: Two values central to the prophets' message
outline.gist: Responsibility and stewardship may not hold the same centrality in other world religions.

outline.heading: Responsibility comes first
outline.gist: One can be responsible without being a steward, but stewardship cannot exist without responsibility.

outline.heading: Looking back and looking forward
outline.gist: Responsibility covers past acts and future duties, while stewardship looks forward; philosophers see both as the burden of being a self.

outline.heading: From mine to entrusted
outline.gist: We teach children that their toy is entrusted to them but forget that our homes, families and jobs are also trusts from Allah.

outline.heading: Power without stewardship
outline.gist: Power without responsibility is volatile; the world needs stewards of intelligence more than artificial intelligence.

outline.heading: What are we in the ecosystem?
outline.gist: Every creature fits its place; humans must ask whether they are members, masters or managers.

outline.heading: With power comes obligation
outline.gist: Free will and intelligence oblige humans to use their power responsibly.

outline.heading: Changing the environment and answering for it
outline.gist: Animals adapt over millions of years while humans reshape their surroundings, perhaps too much, and will be asked about it.

outline.heading: A khalifah on earth
outline.gist: Right after the opening of Al-Baqarah, Allah declares a steward on earth; earth, not Paradise, was always the plan.

outline.heading: Ibrahim made an imam
outline.gist: A steward is responsible for others' wellbeing on behalf of Someone else; what he holds is not his.

outline.heading: Successors so Allah sees how you act
outline.gist: Nations are made successors to be tested on what they do with their power.

outline.heading: Each of you is a shepherd
outline.gist: Ra'i means caregiver: the man at home, the woman in her house, the leader of his people, all will be questioned.

outline.heading: Plant the sapling as the Hour comes
outline.gist: Do your part however small, within the reach you have been given.

outline.heading: It starts with yourself, but does not end there
outline.gist: Some took the verse on minding oneself to mean no responsibility for others; Abu Bakr corrected that reading.

outline.heading: The ship: sail together or sink together
outline.gist: Those on the lower deck drilling a hole sink everyone unless others stop them.

outline.heading: We would rather not be responsible
outline.gist: People accept responsibility for themselves only to keep their freedom; Allah alone is not questioned, and this job description gives a Muslim his meaning.

outline.heading: The widening wingspan
outline.gist: Care grows from self to siblings, spouse, children, extended family, employees and community as Allah grants more.

outline.heading: The opposite is indifference
outline.gist: The first time the companions heard 'khalifah', they learned that 'not my problem' does not work.

outline.heading: Good and bad not caring
outline.gist: Not caring about people's opinions is admirable; not caring about moral responsibility is not.

outline.heading: Dawud, the model steward
outline.gist: Prophet, king, commander, craftsman, singer of the Zabur, judge, husband and father: he held the widest span of roles.

outline.heading: Caregivers of earth and creatures
outline.gist: Animals cannot make laws to avoid extinction; humans can protect them or destroy them and each other.

outline.heading: Umar and the stumbling animal
outline.gist: People in power today lack stewardship; Umar lay awake fearing he would be asked about an unpaved road.

outline.heading: Raising children as caregivers
outline.gist: Children must grow up knowing they are responsible for everything entrusted to them.

59alS6BlE-0.title: Second Week of Ramadan: Establishing the New Standard
59alS6BlE-0.one_line: Use the second week of Ramadan to build new lifelong standards by modelling your ordinary day on the Prophet's ordinary day, imitating him partially where you cannot fully.
59alS6BlE-0.summary: Starting from 2:183, fasting was prescribed so that you may attain taqwa, he notes how the Quran attaches purposes to its commands and makes Ramadan's purpose the forced change of habits. After one week the anxiety of working while fasting is gone, and this is exactly when people start dropping off taraweeh; instead it is the time to build a new standard. His method is to take a snapshot of the Prophet's ordinary day, not a battle or an Eid. He recalls mulazamah, the practice of living with a scholar for weeks, which he did at sixteen with Sheikh Shukri, who barely ate or slept and filled every half hour of transit with dhikr; anyone can act well for a day, but the mask drops after weeks, and the Sahabah lived with the Prophet for years. He then walks through the Prophet's day from several narrations: Isha, a late conversation with Abu Bakr or family, early sleep in the pattern of Dawud, never a whole night awake, Fajr in congregation, the markets after Fajr, walking with widows and the poor, a midday rest, chores at home, and dhikr, dua, visits and smiles as the fillers that made ordinary days extraordinary. He warns against 3 a.m. qiyam followed by seven coffees. In the second khutbah he quotes Aisha that none can match the Prophet's capacity, so imitate partially: ten minutes before Fajr, three fasts a month, a moist tongue. Unlike ascetics who lost moderation, his life was normal yet full of Allah.

outline.heading: Opening
Fasting prescribed so that you may attain taqwa
outline.gist: 2:183, then the Quran's recurring 'so that you may' clauses (attain taqwa, be guided, remember, reason, succeed, be rightly guided, reflect) show that its commands come with stated purposes.

outline.heading: Week two: the fear is gone, time to build
outline.gist: After a week of fasting at work there is no more anxiety and Allah has granted a new peace, yet this is when people start dropping off taraweeh. No excuses: this is the time to build new standards and a new way of life.

outline.heading: A snapshot of the Prophet's ordinary day
outline.gist: Not a battle day or an Eid, but how he spent his normal 24 hours across his life. None of us can live exactly as he did, but Ramadan offers a unique chance to adjust towards it.

outline.heading: Mulazamah with Sheikh Shukri
outline.gist: Living with a scholar for weeks: at sixteen he waited for Sheikh Shukri to visit his daughter so he could eat a whole chicken and sleep, because the sheikh barely ate or slept and filled every idle half hour in transit with dhikr or Quran. Anyone can act well for a day; over weeks the mask drops.

outline.heading: Ramadan is not at your whim
outline.gist: The Sahabah had years of companionship with the Prophet. Ramadan imposes changes whether you like it or not, to drop bad habits and pick up new ones: zoom out on your life, pick what to improve, and come one step closer to his lifestyle every year.

outline.heading: After Isha: staying up with Abu Bakr
outline.gist: Umar's report that the Prophet would pray Isha and then stay up with Abu Bakr over some matter of the Muslims; he was sent to all of humanity and carried its affairs.

outline.heading: Evening talk with family
outline.gist: Aisha: he would go to one of his wives' houses where people gathered and he would talk with them, then retire to his bed.

outline.heading: Early sleep and the prayer of Dawud
outline.gist: He slept in the first part of the night and followed Dawud's pattern: sleep half the night, pray a third, sleep a sixth, so in a hypothetical ten-hour night most is sleep, then prayer, then a little more sleep before Fajr.

outline.heading: Never a whole night: the 3 a.m. trap
outline.gist: Night prayer always came after sleep; Aisha: he never stood a whole night in prayer. Staying up until 3 a.m. in Ramadan and then chugging seven coffees to get through school is not his way and will catch up with you.

outline.heading: Sleep after taraweeh, rise before Fajr
outline.gist: Bad sleep hygiene takes away years, mental health and physical health, even from those in their twenties who feel invincible. Go home and sleep after taraweeh, wake a little before Fajr for a few rak'ahs, and pray Fajr in congregation.

outline.heading: After Fajr: the markets
outline.gist: Al-Nasa'i's narration: he went to the markets of the Muslims, commanding, forbidding, advising, settling matters between them, teaching halal and haram and meeting their needs.

outline.heading: Much dhikr, short khutbahs, walking with the widow
outline.gist: Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa: he made much dhikr and little idle talk, lengthened the prayer and shortened the khutbah, and never disdained walking with a widow or a poor person to settle their need.

outline.heading: Midday rest and work at home
outline.gist: A midday rest, hard to fit into today's workforce, then home: Aisha describes him visiting the sick, milking his goat, mending his sandal, serving his family and patching his garment until Maghrib.

outline.heading: What made his ordinary days different: the fillers
outline.gist: Most days, his included, are ordinary; he had extraordinary days running a new state everyone wanted to destroy, but what set his days apart were the fillers: subhanallah, alhamdulillah, la ilaha illallah, Allahu akbar, hasbiyallah, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah, dua, and time given to people.

outline.heading: A face that was always smiling
outline.gist: He was bright-faced, smiling and joking with people despite the burdens he carried from every side, so the companions knew something was wrong on the rare days his face changed.

outline.heading: Your day: a new standard that outlasts Eid
outline.gist: Look at your day and ask what you can improve and what Ramadan has already improved. Do not flip back to how things were on the day of Eid. Mindfulness means not being distracted from Allah; it feels hard at first for a heart not yet mindful of Him.

outline.heading: Second khutbah: imitate him partially
outline.gist: Aisha: none of you can bear what the Prophet bore. Full imitation is too hard for his followers, but partial imitation is possible: what cannot be attained wholly should not be abandoned wholly.

outline.heading: Ramadan compels change
outline.gist: One purpose of the month is that Allah forces us to change our habits: suhoor breaks your sleep, a day without food changes metabolism, slows you down and reins in desire, and nearly everyone prays some taraweeh. Let it build a system of life resembling his.

outline.heading: Substitutes within reach
outline.gist: Ten minutes before Fajr instead of a third of the night; three fasts a month or Mondays and Thursdays instead of alternate days; a tongue kept moist with dhikr and Quran; spare time filled with visiting the sick, kinship, advice and meeting someone's need.

outline.heading: Ascetics who lost moderation
outline.gist: Buddhist monks and Hindu ascetics live lives no sane person could, without food, drink, marriage or speech, because they lost the middle way. He fasted and ate, slept, married, joked and laughed with his family, yet his life was full of love of Allah.

outline.heading: Small changes, not back-breaking ones
outline.gist: He is not asking for changes that break your back or ruin your family life, only the small ones Ramadan offers, to build and establish the new standard.

outline.heading: Outro

36:34.en: And We have placed therein gardens of the date-palm and grapes, and We have caused springs of water to gush forth therein

36:35.ar: لِيَأۡكُلُواْ مِن ثَمَرِهِۦ وَمَا عَمِلَتۡهُ أَيۡدِيهِمۡۚ أَفَلَا يَشۡكُرُونَ
36:35.en: That they may eat of the fruit thereof, and their hands made it not. Will they not, then, give thanks

36:36.ar: سُبۡحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَ ٱلۡأَزۡوَٰجَ كُلَّهَا مِمَّا تُنۢبِتُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ وَمِنۡ أَنفُسِهِمۡ وَمِمَّا لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
36:36.en: Glory be to Him Who created all the sexual pairs, of that which the earth groweth, and of themselves, and of that which they know not

36:37.ar: وَءَايَةࣱ لَّهُمُ ٱلَّيۡلُ نَسۡلَخُ مِنۡهُ ٱلنَّهَارَ فَإِذَا هُم مُّظۡلِمُونَ
36:37.en: A token unto them is night. We strip it of the day, and lo! they are in darkness

36:38.ar: وَٱلشَّمۡسُ تَجۡرِي لِمُسۡتَقَرࣲّ لَّهَاۚ ذَٰلِكَ تَقۡدِيرُ ٱلۡعَزِيزِ ٱلۡعَلِيمِ
36:38.en: And the sun runneth on unto a resting-place for him. That is the measuring of the Mighty, the Wise

36:39.ar: وَٱلۡقَمَرَ قَدَّرۡنَٰهُ مَنَازِلَ حَتَّىٰ عَادَ كَٱلۡعُرۡجُونِ ٱلۡقَدِيمِ
36:39.en: And for the moon We have appointed mansions till she return like an old shrivelled palm-leaf

36:40.ar: لَا ٱلشَّمۡسُ يَنۢبَغِي لَهَآ أَن تُدۡرِكَ ٱلۡقَمَرَ وَلَا ٱلَّيۡلُ سَابِقُ ٱلنَّهَارِۚ وَكُلࣱّ فِي فَلَكࣲ يَسۡبَحُونَ
36:40.en: It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day. They float each in an orbit

36:41.ar: وَءَايَةࣱ لَّهُمۡ أَنَّا حَمَلۡنَا ذُرِّيَّتَهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡفُلۡكِ ٱلۡمَشۡحُونِ
36:41.en: And a token unto them is that We bear their offspring in the laden ship

36:42.ar: وَخَلَقۡنَا لَهُم مِّن مِّثۡلِهِۦ مَا يَرۡكَبُونَ
36:42.en: And have created for them of the like thereof whereon they ride

36:43.ar: وَإِن نَّشَأۡ نُغۡرِقۡهُمۡ فَلَا صَرِيخَ لَهُمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يُنقَذُونَ
36:43.en: And if We will, We drown them, and there is no help for them, neither can they be saved

36:44.ar: إِلَّا رَحۡمَةࣰ مِّنَّا وَمَتَٰعًا إِلَىٰ حِينࣲ‏
36:44.en: Unless by mercy from Us and as comfort for a while

uSdlFO4fnQw.title: Tafseer of Surat Yasin, Part 4 (33-44)
uSdlFO4fnQw.one_line: Three signs that bring a heart to life: the revived earth, the precise heavens, and the ark, with what saying Subhan Allah truly means.
uSdlFO4fnQw.summary: After the believer's story, he says the surah now teaches how to gain a living heart, starting with noticing Allah's signs. The signs are simple and need no degree, only attention we have dulled, just as we take family for granted and resent our children for taking their privileges for granted. He urges using fasting days to sit outside and contemplate, lamenting a generation that has lost daydreaming to screens. The first passage is the dead earth given life: you plant and water, but you cannot make the seed grow, so be grateful, and know Allah can revive a dead heart the same way. He then explains Subhan Allah as the Muslim's core stance: Allah is not questioned; you question yourself and change what you can, and this protects the soul in times of grief. The second passage looks upward: night drawn out of day, the sun's course, the moon's phases like a dried palm stalk, all in precise orbits without which no life would exist, and none of it under our control. The third passage turns to history: the ark of Nuh and the ships that let humanity travel and share knowledge, things that need not have worked. He lists life, the universe, history and personal experience as sources of iman pointing to one Creator, and asks people to stop and appreciate before rushing on.

outline.heading: The believer lived by different values
outline.gist: His choice was hard to justify rationally because he lived by values most people have not embraced; no one had to assign him responsibility.

outline.heading: What the Prophet brought: spiritual life
outline.gist: The companions were physically alive but had never tasted spiritual life; once they did, it was hard to go back.

outline.heading: Heraclius and Abu Sufyan: faith that mixes with the heart
outline.gist: Heraclius learned that no follower left the Prophet's religion, because faith once mixed with the heart is never given up.

outline.heading: A living heart starts by recognizing signs
outline.gist: The signs need no degree, only the attentiveness most of us outgrow or become numb to.

outline.heading: Taking family and privilege for granted
outline.gist: We take spouses, children and parents for granted, and dislike it when our children ignore privileges that are not the norm in the world.

outline.heading: Use the fasting day to contemplate
outline.gist: Not looking down at food leaves time to look up; sit outside and actually think about what you see every day.

outline.heading: The lost art of daydreaming
outline.gist: He misses staring at rain or clouds; this generation is deprived of simply observing because of screens.

outline.heading: The dead earth brought to life, like a dead heart
outline.gist: Just as Allah revives dead earth and brings grain from it, He can revive a heart, and others will benefit from it.

outline.heading: Gardens and springs not made by their hands
outline.gist: He weighs the reading that their hands made it and prefers that they did not make it, given the call to gratitude that follows.

outline.heading: What if the seed does not grow?
outline.gist: Farmers control everything except the one thing all else rests on, that the seed sprouts; whose laws are these?

outline.heading: He can bring your heart to life too
outline.gist: The verse began with Allah giving life so that you do not despair of your own heart.

outline.heading: Exalted is He who created all pairs
outline.gist: Subhan means Allah is flawless, the source of all good; He created pairs in plants, people and things we do not know.

outline.heading: Subhan Allah: question yourself, not Allah
outline.gist: The Muslim's distinctive view of the divine: Allah is beyond our standards; when something is wrong you question yourself and change what you can.

outline.heading: Tasbih protects you in times of sorrow
outline.gist: Repeating Subhan Allah trains the self not to turn on Allah when pain comes, accepting His decree in ease and difficulty.

outline.heading: We are being tested, not Allah
outline.gist: The Prophet lived magnifying Allah; life is a trial of our role, not of how well God manages the universe.

outline.heading: Nature documentaries as religious time
outline.gist: He has his children watch biology documentaries because observing creation fills you with awe at its depth and variety.

outline.heading: Night stripped from the day: darkness is the norm
outline.gist: Night is drawn out like an animal shedding its skin; outside the atmosphere darkness is the norm and daylight the exception.

outline.heading: The sun runs to its resting place; al-Aziz, the unfathomable
outline.gist: Whatever you can break down and fully understand is a creation, not God.

outline.heading: The moon's phases and the old palm stalk
outline.gist: Months come from the moon, which returns to a crescent like a dried, curved palm branch.

outline.heading: Sun and moon each swimming in its orbit
outline.gist: The sun will not overtake the moon nor night overpower day; each moves in its own course.

outline.heading: A delicate balance that makes life possible
outline.gist: Precise distances and orbits allow life; far from the equator life is harder and depression higher, as winters here show.

outline.heading: A source of energy you do not control
outline.gist: The sun blasts the earth with energy every day; if it failed to rise, all our quarrels would stop, yet we take it for granted.

outline.heading: Seeing a sign, not just the sun
outline.gist: The life of the heart is seeing the sun as a sign of Allah, all of it placed in your service.

outline.heading: The sources of iman all point to one Creator
outline.gist: Life, the universe, history and personal experience each point in the same direction, toward one Creator.

outline.heading: We carried their ancestors in the laden ark
outline.gist: Humanity survives through those carried with Nuh; the history of our existence is itself a sign.

outline.heading: Shared basics across world religions
outline.gist: Faiths with no contact share a creator, reward and punishment, a first couple and a first sin, because the history is the same.

outline.heading: Vessels like the ark to carry them
outline.gist: Allah made ships so people could cross continents, discover places and meet others.

outline.heading: If We willed, We would drown them: why does anything float?
outline.gist: Buoyancy is His law; had it not held, no travel or exchange of knowledge would exist. He lets us enjoy it out of mercy for a time.

outline.heading: Travel, look and appreciate first
outline.gist: See the world's diversity and pause to appreciate it before the restaurant; do not keep the trait you dislike in your children.

outline.heading: Precisely placed for you
outline.gist: He reviews the revived land, the right-sized sun and single moon, and the ships, none of which you planned.

outline.heading: How to gain the believer's life
outline.gist: After the man who was killed yet is alive, Allah shows the way to that life: start by appreciating His signs.

themes.label: Contemplating Allah's signs in creation (tafakkur)
themes.note: A living heart begins by noticing simple signs: the revived earth, the heavens' precision and the ships.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation
themes.note: We control none of what sustains us, from sprouting seeds to sunrise, so at least be grateful.

themes.label: Family: parents, relatives, kinship ties
themes.note: Taking spouses, parents and children for granted, and children taking privilege for granted.

themes.label: Technology, AI, social media and attention
themes.note: Screens have deprived a generation of daydreaming and observation.

themes.label: The Names and Attributes of Allah
themes.note: Subhan as declaring Allah flawless and beyond our standards; al-Aziz as the unfathomable whose essence cannot be broken down.

themes.label: Contentment and acceptance (ridha)
themes.note: Do not question Allah in pain; question yourself, change what you can and accept His decree.

themes.label: Eman: faith, certainty, doubt
themes.note: Life, the universe, history and experience as sources of iman all pointing to one Creator.

hadith.gist: Heraclius asked Abu Sufyan whether any of the Prophet's followers left his religion; told no, he said that is how faith is once its joy mixes with the heart.

9:64.ar: يَحۡذَرُ ٱلۡمُنَٰفِقُونَ أَن تُنَزَّلَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ سُورَةࣱ تُنَبِّئُهُم بِمَا فِي قُلُوبِهِمۡۚ قُلِ ٱسۡتَهۡزِءُوٓاْ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ مُخۡرِجࣱ مَّا تَحۡذَرُونَ
9:64.en: The hypocrites fear lest a surah should be revealed concerning them, proclaiming what is in their hearts. Say: Scoff (your fill)! Lo! Allah is disclosing what ye fear

9:65.ar: وَلَئِن سَأَلۡتَهُمۡ لَيَقُولُنَّ إِنَّمَا كُنَّا نَخُوضُ وَنَلۡعَبُۚ قُلۡ أَبِٱللَّهِ وَءَايَٰتِهِۦ وَرَسُولِهِۦ كُنتُمۡ تَسۡتَهۡزِءُونَ
9:65.en: And if thou ask them (O Muhammad) they will say: We did but talk and jest. Say: Was it at Allah and His revelations and His messenger that ye did scoff

9:66.ar: لَا تَعۡتَذِرُواْ قَدۡ كَفَرۡتُم بَعۡدَ إِيمَٰنِكُمۡۚ إِن نَّعۡفُ عَن طَآئِفَةࣲ مِّنكُمۡ نُعَذِّبۡ طَآئِفَةَۢ بِأَنَّهُمۡ كَانُواْ مُجۡرِمِينَ
9:66.en: Make no excuse. Ye have disbelieved after your (confession of) belief. If We forgive a party of you, a party of you We shall punish because they have been guilty

9:101.ar: وَمِمَّنۡ حَوۡلَكُم مِّنَ ٱلۡأَعۡرَابِ مُنَٰفِقُونَۖ وَمِنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ مَرَدُواْ عَلَى ٱلنِّفَاقِ لَا تَعۡلَمُهُمۡۖ نَحۡنُ نَعۡلَمُهُمۡۚ سَنُعَذِّبُهُم مَّرَّتَيۡنِ ثُمَّ يُرَدُّونَ إِلَىٰ عَذَابٍ عَظِيمࣲ‏
9:101.en: And among those around you of the wandering Arabs there are hypocrites, and among the townspeople of Al-Madinah (there are some who) persist in hypocrisy whom thou (O Muhammad) knowest not. We, We know them, and We shall chastise them twice; then they will be relegated to a painful doom

9:102.ar: وَءَاخَرُونَ ٱعۡتَرَفُواْ بِذُنُوبِهِمۡ خَلَطُواْ عَمَلࣰ ا صَٰلِحࣰ ا وَءَاخَرَ سَيِّئًا عَسَى ٱللَّهُ أَن يَتُوبَ عَلَيۡهِمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمٌ
9:102.en: And (there are) others who have acknowledged their faults. They mixed a righteous action with another that was bad. It may be that Allah will relent toward them. Lo! Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

9:103.ar: خُذۡ مِنۡ أَمۡوَٰلِهِمۡ صَدَقَةࣰ تُطَهِّرُهُمۡ وَتُزَكِّيهِم بِهَا وَصَلِّ عَلَيۡهِمۡۖ إِنَّ صَلَوٰتَكَ سَكَنࣱ لَّهُمۡۗ وَٱللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ
9:103.en: Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow, and pray for them. Lo! thy prayer is an assuagement for them. Allah is Hearer, Knower

9:104.ar: أَلَمۡ يَعۡلَمُوٓاْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ يَقۡبَلُ ٱلتَّوۡبَةَ عَنۡ عِبَادِهِۦ وَيَأۡخُذُ ٱلصَّدَقَٰتِ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
9:104.en: Know they not that Allah is He Who accepteth repentance from His bondmen and taketh the alms, and that Allah is He Who is the Relenting, the Merciful

9:105.ar: وَقُلِ ٱعۡمَلُواْ فَسَيَرَى ٱللَّهُ عَمَلَكُمۡ وَرَسُولُهُۥ وَٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَۖ وَسَتُرَدُّونَ إِلَىٰ عَٰلِمِ ٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
9:105.en: And say (unto them): Act! Allah will behold your actions, and (so will) His messenger and the believers, and ye will be brought back to the Knower of the Invisible and the Visible, and He will tell you what ye used to do

9:106.ar: وَءَاخَرُونَ مُرۡجَوۡنَ لِأَمۡرِ ٱللَّهِ إِمَّا يُعَذِّبُهُمۡ وَإِمَّا يَتُوبُ عَلَيۡهِمۡۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمࣱ‏
9:106.en: And (there are) others who await Allah's decree, whether He will punish them or will forgive them. Allah is Knower, Wise

9:117.ar: لَّقَد تَّابَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَى ٱلنَّبِيِّ وَٱلۡمُهَٰجِرِينَ وَٱلۡأَنصَارِ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوهُ فِي سَاعَةِ ٱلۡعُسۡرَةِ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ مَا كَادَ يَزِيغُ قُلُوبُ فَرِيقࣲ مِّنۡهُمۡ ثُمَّ تَابَ عَلَيۡهِمۡۚ إِنَّهُۥ بِهِمۡ رَءُوفࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
9:117.en: Allah hath turned in mercy to the Prophet, and to the Muhajirin and the Ansar who followed him in the hour of hardship. After the hearts of a party of them had almost swerved aside, then turned He unto them in mercy. Lo! He is Full of Pity, Merciful for them

9:118.ar: وَعَلَى ٱلثَّلَٰثَةِ ٱلَّذِينَ خُلِّفُواْ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا ضَاقَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ بِمَا رَحُبَتۡ وَضَاقَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمۡ أَنفُسُهُمۡ وَظَنُّوٓاْ أَن لَّا مَلۡجَأَ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ إِلَّآ إِلَيۡهِ ثُمَّ تَابَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ لِيَتُوبُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
9:118.en: And to the three also (did He turn in mercy) who were left behind, when the earth, vast as it is, was straitened for them, and their own souls were straitened for them till they bethought them that there is no refuge from Allah save toward Him. Then turned He unto them in mercy that they (too) might turn (repentant unto Him). Lo! Allah! He is the Relenting, the Merciful

9:119.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَكُونُواْ مَعَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ
9:119.en: O ye who believe! Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful

Gjj4y3FE1VQ.title: Tawbah (Ramadan 2026, Night 10: Quranic Themes 2)
Gjj4y3FE1VQ.one_line: What real repentance requires, read through three passages of Surat al-Tawbah: the mocking hypocrites, the three groups around Medina, and Ka'b ibn Malik.
Gjj4y3FE1VQ.summary: He opens by defining tawbah: not carried guilt but an honest admission that something was wrong, real remorse, and a plan, however imperfect, to remove at least one factor that makes the sin easy. Repentance without these is not serious, which is why people who never believed their habit was a problem relapse. He then reads rarely explained verses about hypocrites who mocked Allah, His signs and His Prophet and called it a joke. Allah refused their apology, even though the door of repentance stays open until death, because mocking the sacred needs full repentance, a turning of one's whole life. He tells young people to leave gatherings where the deen is mocked, and recounts the hadith of the man who found his lost camel to show Allah's joy at repentance. The verses about the people around Medina describe three groups: entrenched hypocrites who are dead weight in a community, those who admit their sins and mix good with bad, and the indifferent whose fate is deferred. He asks everyone to give more than they take and to be in the middle group. The story of Ka'b ibn Malik closes the night: he refused to lie, endured fifty days of boycott, burned a king's invitation, and found that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him.

outline.heading: Remorse, not guilt
outline.gist: Tawbah is an acknowledgement that what you did was wrong, producing useful remorse; people who relapse after rehab often never believed their habit was a problem.

outline.heading: Tawbah needs a plan
outline.gist: Without remorse and a plan you will go back; the plan need not be perfect but must remove at least one factor that makes the sin easy, such as time with a certain person. Wrongs against people need restitution, a separate topic.

outline.heading: Hypocrites fear being exposed
outline.gist: Heavy verses rarely explained: the hypocrites feared a surah revealing what was in their hearts, and Allah exposes them, often through their own behaviour, because the mask eventually falls.

outline.heading: 'We were only joking'
outline.gist: Asked about their mockery, they said they were just playing; he asks why, of everything one could laugh at, they chose Allah, His signs and His Prophet.

outline.heading: Leave gatherings that mock the deen
outline.gist: He tells young people to walk away from groups that belittle Allah, the Prophet or the deen, without picking fights, because the next verse treats such mockery as disbelief; the hypocrites only went along with religion for social reasons.

outline.heading: When an apology is not accepted
outline.gist: The door of tawbah is open until death and until the sun rises from the west, yet here Allah says 'make no excuse': mocking the divine needs repentance, not a quick apology.

outline.heading: Tawbah is turning your life around
outline.gist: Tawbah means deciding you are done, turning the ship around and planning to stay on course; nothing Allah granted us is more beautiful.

outline.heading: The man who found his lost camel
outline.gist: A man stranded in the desert lies in a grave he dug, then his camel returns with food and water; Allah is happier with your repentance than he was.

outline.heading: Hypocrites among the Bedouins and Medina
outline.gist: Some around Medina pledged allegiance only for protection and benefits like zakat.

outline.heading: Dead weight in a community
outline.gist: Hypocrites inflate the numbers but are absent when money, volunteers or experts are needed, then demand service and complain about the facility; the Prophet himself saw half his people stay back.

outline.heading: Always give more than you take
outline.gist: In communal work everyone must contribute more than they receive; only the youth may take more, so they can build their character before they give.

outline.heading: Our real problems are internal
outline.gist: Entrenched hypocrisy is punished twice because it rots the ummah from within; our defeats come from ourselves, not our enemies.

outline.heading: Those who admit their sins: that's us
outline.gist: Another group admits their sins and mixes good with bad, and Allah may forgive them; scholars wept and spent whole nights repeating this verse.

outline.heading: The deferred group: the indifferent
outline.gist: A third group neither repents nor commits; they drift through life and their judgment is left to Allah.

outline.heading: Tabuk: the hour of difficulty
outline.gist: Allah accepted the repentance of the Prophet and all who marched to Tabuk in heat, hunger and poverty, because everyone always needs tawbah.

outline.heading: The excuses of those who stayed behind
outline.gist: On the return most of those who stayed home came with excuses, some true and many false, and the Prophet prayed for their forgiveness.

outline.heading: Ka'b ibn Malik: no excuse at all
outline.gist: Three men stayed back with no excuse; one was Ka'b, a famous poet and an early Muslim who had been present at a decisive moment in Islam's history.

outline.heading: Ka'b chooses the truth
outline.gist: A gifted speaker who could talk his way out with anyone else, Ka'b told the Prophet the truth knowing revelation would expose a lie; honesty earns no medal, it is simply the only way to live.

outline.heading: Fifty days of boycott
outline.gist: Ka'b and the two others were shunned for fifty days, the length of the Tabuk expedition, with no one speaking or returning their salams.

outline.heading: The king's letter
outline.gist: A king invited Ka'b to his court; he wept that Allah's enemies now saw weakness in him, and burned the letter.

outline.heading: The day of acceptance
outline.gist: Everyone makes mistakes; on the fiftieth day the verses came, the Prophet called it the best day of Ka'b's life, and the Muslims embraced him.

outline.heading: No refuge from Allah except in Him
outline.gist: The vast earth felt narrow and their chests tight until they realised there is no running away from Allah, only running back to Him.

im7_zZK6pnE.title: Ramadan 2026, Night 8: Quranic Themes 2 - Demise of the Vain
im7_zZK6pnE.one_line: How vanity clouds judgment and destroys people, read through Adam's deception, Thamud's arrogant leaders and Allah withholding His signs from the arrogant.
im7_zZK6pnE.summary: He defines the vain as those who overestimate themselves and their deeds, and argues that once vanity takes hold every later judgment is built on a false starting point. The cure is an accurate view: every human has a fixed divine value that no status can raise and no humiliation can lower, which is why slavery and racism are false, but our efforts really are flawed and mediocre, and admitting that is the only path to growth. Valuing our own deeds trespasses on Allah's role as their judge. In Al-A'raf, Shaytan swore he was a sincere adviser and led Adam and Hawwa like a carrot, exploiting the vanity that bristled at being mortal servants; the exposure of their nakedness is read by scholars as their moral flaws coming to light. They had been warned, which shows that knowing what is right is not enough if an inner weakness remains, so we must trace why we fell and seal the crack. Thamud's arrogant leaders rejected Salih simply because the weak believed in him, then killed the she-camel; the Quraysh likewise demanded separate sessions for nobles. He closes with Allah's statement that He turns the arrogant away from His signs.

outline.heading: The vain: overvaluing oneself and one's deeds
outline.gist: A theme found almost everywhere in the Quran; he returns to vanity and arrogance in every series because the Quran does.

outline.heading: Vanity destroys judgment
outline.gist: An inflated sense of self makes every later assessment false because it rests on a false first premise.

outline.heading: Neither more nor less than a servant
outline.gist: Humans have real divine value but are servants of Allah; the pendulum swinging either way causes trouble.

outline.heading: Divine value versus potential
outline.gist: We come from soil, are flawed and ignorant by nature with great potential; our human value stays the same whether emperor or paraded in disgrace.

outline.heading: Why slavery and racism are false
outline.gist: They claim some people have less human value by nature, which is simply untrue.

outline.heading: Humility is not a lie you tell yourself
outline.gist: Pretending to be less good while believing otherwise masks vanity; the truth is our efforts are flawed, and admitting it is the only way to grow.

outline.heading: Vanity as a pathology
outline.gist: Successful, wealthy, popular people often end up miserable and self-destructive; vanity is a spiritual and psychological disease that brings its own ruin.

outline.heading: Only Allah appraises our deeds
outline.gist: We compete in taqwa and hope Allah values our actions; declaring our own deeds praiseworthy oversteps into His domain.

outline.heading: Shaytan swore he was a sincere adviser
outline.gist: Adam's story recurs across the Quran with deliberate differences; here Shaytan leads them on with what they wanted, like a carrot.

outline.heading: Exploiting the weakness within
outline.gist: Shaytan used no outside force but their inner vanity; the story is the raw human experience, a solved problem for us, not a slight on Adam.

outline.heading: Servant does not sound attractive
outline.gist: Told they were mortal servants, the nafs struck back insisting it was a king, and Shaytan promised them a higher rank.

outline.heading: Led on by delusion
outline.gist: The person full of himself has clouded judgment; their vanity became a barrier that kept them from seeing how they were being played.

outline.heading: Nakedness as exposed flaws
outline.gist: Scholars read the exposure figuratively: their vanity and fear came to light, as shameful as being naked, and covering with leaves of Paradise means its teachings.

outline.heading: They had already been warned
outline.gist: Allah had told them the tree was forbidden and Shaytan their enemy; he once studied the story for weeks assuming they did not know.

outline.heading: Knowing the right thing is not enough
outline.gist: If a weakness remains inside, Shaytan exploits it and you later cannot believe what you did.

outline.heading: Find out why you did it, then seal the crack
outline.gist: Rather than burying a shameful episode, work out exactly what was exploited so it cannot be used again; vanity is a carrot chased for life.

outline.heading: Al-A'raf: succeeding as a community
outline.gist: The surah's prophet stories stress communal worship and success; we cannot afford indifference because we sail or sink together.

outline.heading: Thamud: rich, spoiled and indifferent
outline.gist: Salih's people had great wealth and power and took it for granted when he came to correct them.

outline.heading: The town hall: 'we reject whatever you believe'
outline.gist: The arrogant leaders asked the weak if they had heard of Salih and, on learning they believed, rejected it outright without weighing his character, teaching or miracle.

outline.heading: Too good to be seen with them
outline.gist: Everyone will one day feel tempted to reject something only because a disliked group embraces it; the test is not letting that feeling drive behaviour.

outline.heading: Killing the she-camel and daring the punishment
outline.gist: Their sudden aggression came from refusing to be grouped with the believers.

outline.heading: Quraysh ask for separate sessions for nobles
outline.gist: During the negotiation period the Quraysh offered to follow the Prophet if nobles could be taught apart and stand in front of the slaves.

outline.heading: Only knowledge puts someone up front
outline.gist: Islam is take it or leave it: everyone is equal, lineage counts for nothing, and he hopes someone more knowledgeable will one day replace him.

outline.heading: Interlude
The arrogant are turned away from His signs
outline.gist: Allah states plainly that He will not grant His signs and guidance to the arrogant.

outline.heading: Outro

6SmV1nBWrEo.speaker_note: continues his own Ramadan values series and refers to his earlier tazkiyah series on self-honesty
6SmV1nBWrEo.title: The Values of Islam: Sidq (Honesty) and Amanah (Trustworthiness)
6SmV1nBWrEo.one_line: Honesty is absolute and begins with honesty toward oneself; trustworthiness is honesty plus guarding others' rights, and without both no person or society survives.
6SmV1nBWrEo.summary: The sheikh opens by arguing that Islamic revival means reviving its values, which have never changed from Adam to Muhammad, and that masjids should send children home knowing what they stand for. He then takes honesty and trustworthiness, defined through their opposites, lying and betrayal. Honesty is absolute apart from narrow exceptions such as compliments, war and reconciling people. It starts with self-honesty: a person who lies to himself ends up sincerely telling lies, like those who will swear falsely to Allah on the Day of Judgment. Ka'b ibn Malik's truthfulness after Tabuk shows that honesty earns no reward and may bring hard consequences, yet lies always snap back and multiply into a web. Trustworthiness is honesty combined with preserving others' rights; it takes years to build and one breach to destroy. The Prophet's role at the Black Stone dispute, his challenge at Safa and Ali returning the deposits of his persecutors show his trust. Hypocrisy is the opposite of both. He urges parents to break children's early discovery that lying solves problems, notes that honesty is the door to tawbah, and shows that money, neighbourhoods and the greeting of salam all rest on trust.

outline.heading: Values are what reviving Islam means
outline.gist: Revival is not governance or politics but the ethics Islam came to instill, unchanged from Adam to Muhammad.

outline.heading: What masjids should teach children
outline.gist: The series' framework is for passing on to children, who should leave the masjid clear on their values.

outline.heading: Values known by their opposites
outline.gist: He orders values by importance and introduces honesty and trust through their opposites, lying and betrayal.

outline.heading: Honesty as the most basic value
outline.gist: Some scholars see honesty as the most important value or the one never to be breached.

outline.heading: The narrow exceptions
outline.gist: Compliments, war and reconciling estranged people are not counted as lying; outside them there is no excuse.

outline.heading: Honesty starts with yourself
outline.gist: Lying to yourself means later telling lies you believe, a distortion fixable only by going back to the first lie.

outline.heading: Those who swear falsely to Allah
outline.gist: People will swear on Judgment Day as they swore in this life, believing their own lie; they are the true liars.

outline.heading: Ka'b ibn Malik after Tabuk
outline.gist: He alone with two others admitted he had no excuse and then endured fifty days of boycott.

outline.heading: Honesty is not owed a reward
outline.gist: Expect consequences for admitting a mistake; distorting reality snaps back harder in this life or the next.

outline.heading: The web of lies
outline.gist: One lie needs another to defend it until a person no longer knows what is real; the young should never start.

outline.heading: Honesty forces better choices
outline.gist: Bad choices create the need to lie; committing to honesty pushes you to behave better.

outline.heading: Trust is honesty plus guarding rights
outline.gist: Trust builds over years into a reputation, and one breach ends it.

outline.heading: The Black Stone dispute
outline.gist: The tribes accepted the Prophet's judgment because amanah is how honesty shows itself: one face, one narrative.

outline.heading: Hypocrisy as the opposite
outline.gist: The signs of the hypocrite, lying and betraying, are the reverse of these two values.

outline.heading: Al-Amin of Makkah and the call at Safa
outline.gist: People left their valuables with him and admitted they had never known him to lie in forty years.

outline.heading: Returning the trusts of his persecutors
outline.gist: He left Ali behind to return deposits to the people who tried to kill him; institutions today struggle to earn such trust.

outline.heading: Children discover that lying works
outline.gist: Parents and the community must teach early that lies that solve problems now rot one's ethics.

outline.heading: Truth leads to righteousness
outline.gist: Honesty leads to every virtue and to Paradise; lying leads to fujur, a life without a moral compass.

outline.heading: A believer may slip but will not lie
outline.gist: Admitting what you did is the only path to tawbah and redemption.

outline.heading: Lying to Allah, to yourself, to people
outline.gist: Lying to people is the least of the three and a consequence of the other two lies already told.

outline.heading: Society is built on trust
outline.gist: Money, politics and letting a child walk to school all depend on trust; pre-Islamic Arabia lived without it.

outline.heading: Salam as a declaration of safety
outline.gist: Strangers in the desert met in a showdown until the Prophet introduced a greeting that promises safety.

outline.heading: The untrusted live alone
outline.gist: People who cannot find work, marriage or friends often do not see that others have identified them as dishonest.

outline.heading: The hallmarks of the Prophet's followers
outline.gist: He was the truthful and trustworthy one; without these there is little else to discuss.

yAnWOaJYNjE.title: Those Who Doom Themselves (Ramadan 2026, Night 11: Quranic Themes 2)
yAnWOaJYNjE.one_line: Pharaoh, Nuh's son and the people of Lut as examples of people who doom themselves, and why Muslims must own their choices.
yAnWOaJYNjE.summary: The theme is that Allah never forces anyone into ruin; people bring it on themselves. He ties this to the Islamic sense of personal accountability and argues that Western culture, with its softened feedback and fear of liability, slows young people from owning their lives. He insists our deepest failures are internal: what he once blamed on the Assad regime in his dawah work in Syria, he found unchanged in Canada. Pharaoh is the first example: offered exit after exit, he clung to his position out of ego and invested years, surrounded by enablers, until he declared belief while drowning, too late. He urges the courage to admit long-held mistakes and friends who challenge rather than applaud. The second example, which he calls the saddest story in the Quran, is Nuh calling his isolated son onto the ark. He applies it to teenagers who cut themselves off from family, argues that youth-welcoming masajid would reduce this, contrasts today's library-like masajid with the lived-in masjid of the Prophet, and presses the community to invest in the next generation as the Prophet did with his young companions. The people of Lut, who chose to overturn basic decency and ignored his pleas, are the last example. He closes on the rule that no one dooms you but yourself.

outline.heading: Allah never oppresses: people doom themselves
outline.gist: A recurring Quranic theme: Allah does not force anyone into deviance; whoever ends up in the wrong direction has brought it on himself and has no one else to blame.

outline.heading: Teach responsibility early
outline.gist: We fail to teach children that they own their choices; he knows adults in their fifties and sixties who still blame others. Muslims hand control of their lives to no one, and there is empowerment in that.

outline.heading: A culture that sugarcoats
outline.gist: Canadian and Western culture waters down feedback and fears liability, so young people take longer to accept accountability; everyone faces pushes both ways, and which one you follow is your choice.

outline.heading: Yunus, Hud and Yusuf: a cluster of surahs
outline.gist: These surahs each address a critical domain of faith: reform as the backbone of the message, ethics that stay consistent rather than becoming preferences, and the law that the right thing be done the right way.

outline.heading: Musa's two struggles and the Prophet's
outline.gist: Musa faced an external tyrant and then disobedience among his own followers, mirroring the Prophet's struggle in Mecca and then Medina; the internal struggle is harder.

outline.heading: Our failures are internal
outline.gist: In Syria he blamed the Assad regime for the failures of dawah; in Canada, without that regime, he found the same failures, and learned the problem is within.

outline.heading: Pharaoh pursues and drowns
outline.gist: Pharaoh's army chased Bani Israel across the sea intending harm, and as the sea engulfed him he declared belief in the God of Bani Israel.

outline.heading: 'Now?'
outline.gist: After all the killing, enslavement, years of respite and signs, he submits only as his soul leaves.

outline.heading: His body saved as a sign
outline.gist: Allah preserved his body so later generations would see the man who declared himself the highest lord and ruled by inequality; yet many ignore the signs.

outline.heading: Ego and the courage to admit you were wrong
outline.gist: Pharaoh was offered exits but had invested too much to back down; people stuck for twenty years in a wrong commitment justify it to save face. Someone who can admit they were wrong is rare and worth keeping as a friend.

outline.heading: Enablers and the friend who challenges you
outline.gist: The mind lies to protect us and enablers silence our self-doubt; keep the annoying friend who questions you. Pharaoh's ego held until the water filled his lungs.

outline.heading: Scholars who hope even Pharaoh is saved
outline.gist: Some scholars argue his last words saved him, showing how the hearts of the ummah's scholars lean toward people being saved; but he doomed himself, and the story is told so we avoid his trap.

outline.heading: Nuh: the saddest story in the Quran
outline.gist: Nuh spent centuries calling people with very few followers; what every man wants in the end is his family, and he did everything right for his, but one son would not listen.

outline.heading: The ark and the isolated son
outline.gist: Sailing amid waves like mountains, Nuh sees his son, who stood apart; the word describing him may refer both to that moment and to how he lived.

outline.heading: Young people who isolate themselves
outline.gist: He sees teenagers and students living apart from their families' way of life, and feels for the parents, siblings and the young person alike.

outline.heading: If masajid welcomed youth
outline.gist: Masajid built around serving young people, with space, people and facilities for them and tolerance of their problems, would reduce this isolation, even if it never disappears.

outline.heading: No different in a Damascus suburb
outline.gist: Growing up in a devout Syrian village, few young men prayed in the masjid; at a janazah twice as many stood outside as prayed.

outline.heading: The Prophet's masjid was lived in
outline.gist: Today's masajid are run like libraries that guard architecture and quiet; the Prophet's masjid had people living, eating and caring for children in it.

outline.heading: Open the masjid at least to your own children
outline.gist: He is not asking for extremes, but people harsh toward youth change their minds once they have a thirteen-year-old of their own.

outline.heading: 'I will take refuge on a mountain'
outline.gist: Nuh begs his son to board; the son says a mountain will protect him, a wave comes between them and Nuh watches him drown.

outline.heading: Fathers watching their children drown
outline.gist: Many parents watch the waves of desire and doubt sweep their children away without the tools to help; sending money overseas means little if in thirty years no Muslims are left here.

outline.heading: Invest in the next generation
outline.gist: Educate and empower young Muslims and strengthen their identity, because his generation was crippled by oppression; the Prophet built a foundation of young companions like Ali who carried Islam after him.

outline.heading: The people of Lut chose to corrupt the fitrah
outline.gist: They made a deliberate moral choice to overturn basic human decency and mocked Lut's efforts as outdated, with slogans of openness that have returned today.

outline.heading: Guests at Lut's door
outline.gist: The angels came as handsome young men and the people rushed to Lut's house to reach them.

outline.heading: 'My daughters are purer for you'
outline.gist: Lut meant the women of his nation, through marriage, not his own daughters; he called them back to what is pure and asked them not to shame him before his guests.

outline.heading: 'Is there not one sensible man among you?'
outline.gist: Lut called it a dreadful day because he knew what his people would do; he asked whether anyone with basic common sense and decency remained.

outline.heading: No one dooms you but yourself
outline.gist: They too doomed themselves; whenever the Quran tells of a people destroyed, it is what they brought on themselves, not injustice from Allah.

36:19.ar: قَالُواْ طَٰٓئِرُكُم مَّعَكُمۡ أَئِن ذُكِّرۡتُمۚ بَلۡ أَنتُمۡ قَوۡمࣱ مُّسۡرِفُونَ
36:19.en: They said: Your evil augury be with you! Is it because ye are reminded (of the truth)? Nay, but ye are froward folk

36:20.ar: وَجَآءَ مِنۡ أَقۡصَا ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ رَجُلࣱ يَسۡعَىٰ قَالَ يَٰقَوۡمِ ٱتَّبِعُواْ ٱلۡمُرۡسَلِينَ
36:20.en: And there came from the uttermost part of the city a man running. He cried: O my people! Follow those who have been sent

36:21.ar: ٱتَّبِعُواْ مَن لَّا يَسۡـَٔلُكُمۡ أَجۡرࣰ ا وَهُم مُّهۡتَدُونَ
36:21.en: Follow those who ask of you no fee, and who are rightly guided

36:22.ar: وَمَالِيَ لَآ أَعۡبُدُ ٱلَّذِي فَطَرَنِي وَإِلَيۡهِ تُرۡجَعُونَ
36:22.en: For what cause should I not serve Him Who hath created me, and unto Whom ye will be brought back

36:23.ar: ءَأَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ ءَالِهَةً إِن يُرِدۡنِ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنُ بِضُرࣲّ لَّا تُغۡنِ عَنِّي شَفَٰعَتُهُمۡ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَا يُنقِذُونِ
36:23.en: Shall I take (other) gods in place of Him when, if the Beneficent should wish me any harm, their intercession will avail me naught, nor can they save

36:24.ar: إِنِّيٓ إِذࣰ ا لَّفِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينٍ
36:24.en: Then truly I should be in error manifest

36:25.en: Lo! I have believed in your Lord, so hear me

36:26.ar: قِيلَ ٱدۡخُلِ ٱلۡجَنَّةَۖ قَالَ يَٰلَيۡتَ قَوۡمِي يَعۡلَمُونَ
36:26.en: It was said (unto him): Enter paradise. He said: Would that my people knew

36:27.ar: بِمَا غَفَرَ لِي رَبِّي وَجَعَلَنِي مِنَ ٱلۡمُكۡرَمِينَ
36:27.en: With what (munificence) my Lord hath pardoned me and made me of the honoured ones

36:28.ar: ۞وَمَآ أَنزَلۡنَا عَلَىٰ قَوۡمِهِۦ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦ مِن جُندࣲ مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَمَا كُنَّا مُنزِلِينَ

36:30.ar: يَٰحَسۡرَةً عَلَى ٱلۡعِبَادِۚ مَا يَأۡتِيهِم مِّن رَّسُولٍ إِلَّا كَانُواْ بِهِۦ يَسۡتَهۡزِءُونَ

36:31.ar: أَلَمۡ يَرَوۡاْ كَمۡ أَهۡلَكۡنَا قَبۡلَهُم مِّنَ ٱلۡقُرُونِ أَنَّهُمۡ إِلَيۡهِمۡ لَا يَرۡجِعُونَ

36:32.ar: وَإِن كُلࣱّ لَّمَّا جَمِيعࣱ لَّدَيۡنَا مُحۡضَرُونَ

36:13.ar: وَٱضۡرِبۡ لَهُم مَّثَلًا أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡقَرۡيَةِ إِذۡ جَآءَهَا ٱلۡمُرۡسَلُونَ

36:14.ar: إِذۡ أَرۡسَلۡنَآ إِلَيۡهِمُ ٱثۡنَيۡنِ فَكَذَّبُوهُمَا فَعَزَّزۡنَا بِثَالِثࣲ فَقَالُوٓاْ إِنَّآ إِلَيۡكُم مُّرۡسَلُونَ

36:15.ar: قَالُواْ مَآ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا بَشَرࣱ مِّثۡلُنَا وَمَآ أَنزَلَ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنُ مِن شَيۡءٍ إِنۡ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا تَكۡذِبُونَ
36:15.en: They said: Ye are but mortals like unto us. The Beneficent hath naught revealed. Ye do but lie

36:16.ar: قَالُواْ رَبُّنَا يَعۡلَمُ إِنَّآ إِلَيۡكُمۡ لَمُرۡسَلُونَ

tke5s8G7aFg.title: Tafseer of Surat Yasin, Part 3 (20-32)
tke5s8G7aFg.one_line: The man who came running: a living heart's sense of responsibility, why sacred knowledge is never sold, and 'I wish my people knew'.
tke5s8G7aFg.summary: He recaps the three messengers, calling shirk the root of all evil and noting it includes worship of desire, fame and people. The people's threats show what happens once a line is crossed: it becomes normal, which is why Islam stresses prevention, especially for youth. The heart of the surah is the man who came running from the edge of the city. Logically he had every reason to stay home: three messengers were already there, he lived on the outskirts, and the people were violent. That is the point: a living heart feels responsible for its people, unlike the common Muslim refrain of not wanting to get involved. His first argument, follow those who ask you for no wage, leads to a strong section on sacred knowledge being priceless: charging for it disrespects it, masjids must not be money makers, and the great imams refused payment, Imam Ahmad gleaning fallen wheat for a living. The man affirms tawhid, is killed, and the Quran skips his death to his words in paradise: I wish my people knew. He presents this as the heart fully alive, still wishing good for those who killed him. The people are destroyed by one blast, and Allah laments servants who mock every messenger.

outline.heading: An unnamed believer: why the Quran omits names
outline.gist: The man's name is unknown and irrelevant; leaving it out makes the story universal, a model for every believer.

outline.heading: The life of the heart
outline.gist: True life is inner peace with your choices, your past and silence; those who find it lose interest in everything else.

outline.heading: Recap: three messengers in one township
outline.gist: Three messengers preached together, each confirming the others, against their people's shirk.

outline.heading: Shirk as the root of evil and its many forms
outline.gist: Accepting any second source of values unbalances everything; shirk includes worship of desire, fame and other people.

outline.heading: Your omen is with you; a people who crossed every line
outline.gist: The messengers tell them the bad omen is in their own heads and that they have gone beyond all limits.

outline.heading: Once a line is crossed it is normalized: the value of prevention
outline.gist: Someone who has committed a sin is far likelier to repeat it, so taqwa means prevention, especially keeping youth from zina.

outline.heading: A man came running from the farthest part of the city
outline.gist: He recites the passage and introduces the man who arrives calling his people to follow the messengers.

outline.heading: Why would he come when three messengers were already there?
outline.gist: With three divinely sent messengers in the city, it could seem he had no duty to speak at all.

outline.heading: He lived outside the city among a violent people
outline.gist: He lived on the outskirts, the people threatened even prophets, and logically he had every reason to stay home.

outline.heading: O my people: responsibility and stewardship
outline.gist: That is how a Muslim is supposed to be: he feels innately responsible for his people even if he does not like them.

outline.heading: Threatening messengers signals the end
outline.gist: When a people begin threatening their messengers, divine punishment is near, so he ran as fast as he could.

outline.heading: Every community needs a few hearts like his
outline.gist: A heart alive with love of Allah and not dulled by desire and status cannot watch its people destroy themselves.

outline.heading: Against 'I don't want to get involved'
outline.gist: He could have said he did not belong to the city, the excuse Muslims commonly give about their own communities.

outline.heading: Follow those who ask you for no wage
outline.gist: The Quran repeatedly marks prophets as asking for no money; it is how you know they are genuine.

outline.heading: No secondary gain, and rightly guided
outline.gist: His two reasons: they want nothing from you, no empire or loyalty, and they are people of clear guidance and character.

outline.heading: Allah chooses the noblest as messengers
outline.gist: Messengers come from the best lineage and character so no one can dismiss them for their past.

outline.heading: Sacred knowledge is priceless; his debt to his teachers
outline.gist: Asking money for the deen disrespects it; his own teacher was offended when his father offered a gift after he finished his ijazah.

outline.heading: Masjids cannot be money makers
outline.gist: Not charging for Quran programs is not an experiment but the way of every prophet; people rarely take as a guide someone they pay.

outline.heading: Paid scholars as a late decline; Imam Ahmad gleaning wheat
outline.gist: Historically scholars were independent and refused payment; Imam Ahmad and his family lived by gathering fallen wheat.

outline.heading: Why would I not worship the One who created me
outline.gist: He turns the question on himself: serving his Creator is the obvious choice, and all will return to Him.

outline.heading: Idols whose intercession cannot save
outline.gist: If the Merciful wills harm, other gods cannot help; choosing them would be clear misguidance. He notes a reading pause at the verse end.

outline.heading: I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me
outline.gist: Driven by love for Allah, for dawah and for his people, he declares his faith openly though he gains nothing.

outline.heading: Interlude
Enter paradise: he was killed
outline.gist: Narrations describe a brutal killing; he likely knew it was coming and spoke anyway, and Allah praises him.

outline.heading: I wish my people knew
outline.gist: The Quran skips his death to his words; a young man taken from his family responds only by wishing his people knew of Allah's forgiveness.

outline.heading: A living heart wishes good even for its killers
outline.gist: A heart full of love of Allah keeps empathy for people who wrong it, because they do not know what they are doing.

outline.heading: He died but he is not dead
outline.gist: He is more alive than most of us; his stand made his life worth living.

outline.heading: No army from the sky: one blast and they were still
outline.gist: Allah did not need armies; one cry and they became lifeless.

outline.heading: Arrogance of numbers and alas for the servants
outline.gist: A few people echoing each other feel powerful though wrong; Allah laments servants who mock every messenger.

outline.heading: Fallen nations never return; all will be gathered
outline.gist: Civilizations that took a millennium to build can fall in days and never come back, and all will be brought before Allah.

themes.label: Community building, cooperation and the ummah

themes.label: The masjid: its role and etiquette

6:36.ar: ۞إِنَّمَا يَسۡتَجِيبُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَسۡمَعُونَۘ وَٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰ يَبۡعَثُهُمُ ٱللَّهُ ثُمَّ إِلَيۡهِ يُرۡجَعُونَ
6:36.en: Only those can accept who hear. As for the dead, Allah will raise them up; then unto Him they will be returned

6:37.ar: وَقَالُواْ لَوۡلَا نُزِّلَ عَلَيۡهِ ءَايَةࣱ مِّن رَّبِّهِۦۚ قُلۡ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ قَادِرٌ عَلَىٰٓ أَن يُنَزِّلَ ءَايَةࣰ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
6:37.en: They say: Why hath no portent been sent down upon him from his Lord? Say: Lo! Allah is Able to send down a portent. But most of them know not

6:38.ar: وَمَا مِن دَآبَّةࣲ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَلَا طَٰٓئِرࣲ يَطِيرُ بِجَنَاحَيۡهِ إِلَّآ أُمَمٌ أَمۡثَالُكُمۚ مَّا فَرَّطۡنَا فِي ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ مِن شَيۡءࣲۚ ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِمۡ يُحۡشَرُونَ
6:38.en: There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you. We have neglected nothing in the Book (of Our decrees). Then unto their Lord they will be gathered

6:39.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا صُمࣱّ وَبُكۡمࣱ فِي ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِۗ مَن يَشَإِ ٱللَّهُ يُضۡلِلۡهُ وَمَن يَشَأۡ يَجۡعَلۡهُ عَلَىٰ صِرَٰطࣲ مُّسۡتَقِيمࣲ‏
6:39.en: Those who deny Our revelations are deaf and dumb in darkness. Whom Allah will sendeth astray, and whom He will He placeth on a straight path

6:83.ar: وَتِلۡكَ حُجَّتُنَآ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهَآ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ عَلَىٰ قَوۡمِهِۦۚ نَرۡفَعُ دَرَجَٰتࣲ مَّن نَّشَآءُۗ إِنَّ رَبَّكَ حَكِيمٌ عَلِيمࣱ‏
6:83.en: That is Our argument. We gave it unto Abraham against his folk. We raise unto degrees of wisdom whom We will. Lo! thy Lord is Wise, Aware

6:84.ar: وَوَهَبۡنَا لَهُۥٓ إِسۡحَٰقَ وَيَعۡقُوبَۚ كُلًّا هَدَيۡنَاۚ وَنُوحًا هَدَيۡنَا مِن قَبۡلُۖ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِهِۦ دَاوُۥدَ وَسُلَيۡمَٰنَ وَأَيُّوبَ وَيُوسُفَ وَمُوسَىٰ وَهَٰرُونَۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجۡزِي ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
6:84.en: And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob; each of them We guided; and Noah did We guide aforetime; and of his seed (We guided) David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the good

6:85.ar: وَزَكَرِيَّا وَيَحۡيَىٰ وَعِيسَىٰ وَإِلۡيَاسَۖ كُلࣱّ مِّنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
6:85.en: And Zachariah and John and Jesus and Elias. Each one (of them) was of the righteous

6:86.ar: وَإِسۡمَٰعِيلَ وَٱلۡيَسَعَ وَيُونُسَ وَلُوطࣰ اۚ وَكُلࣰّ ا فَضَّلۡنَا عَلَى ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
6:86.en: And Ishmael and Elisha and Jonah and Lot. Each one (of them) did We prefer above (Our) creatures

6:87.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَابَآئِهِمۡ وَذُرِّيَّٰتِهِمۡ وَإِخۡوَٰنِهِمۡۖ وَٱجۡتَبَيۡنَٰهُمۡ وَهَدَيۡنَٰهُمۡ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطࣲ مُّسۡتَقِيمࣲ‏
6:87.en: With some of their forefathers and their offspring and their brethren; and We chose them and guided them unto a straight path

6:88.ar: ذَٰلِكَ هُدَى ٱللَّهِ يَهۡدِي بِهِۦ مَن يَشَآءُ مِنۡ عِبَادِهِۦۚ وَلَوۡ أَشۡرَكُواْ لَحَبِطَ عَنۡهُم مَّا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ
6:88.en: Such is the guidance of Allah wherewith He guideth whom He will of His bondmen. But if they had set up (for worship) aught beside Him, (all) that they did would have been vain

6:89.ar: أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحُكۡمَ وَٱلنُّبُوَّةَۚ فَإِن يَكۡفُرۡ بِهَا هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ فَقَدۡ وَكَّلۡنَا بِهَا قَوۡمࣰ ا لَّيۡسُواْ بِهَا بِكَٰفِرِينَ
6:89.en: Those are they unto whom We gave the Scripture and command and prophethood. But if these disbelieve therein, then indeed We shall entrust it to a people who will not be disbelievers therein

6:90.ar: أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ هَدَى ٱللَّهُۖ فَبِهُدَىٰهُمُ ٱقۡتَدِهۡۗ قُل لَّآ أَسۡـَٔلُكُمۡ عَلَيۡهِ أَجۡرًاۖ إِنۡ هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكۡرَىٰ لِلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
6:90.en: Those are they whom Allah guideth, so follow their guidance. Say (O Muhammad, unto mankind): I ask of you no fee for it. Lo! it is naught but a Reminder to (His) creatures

6:141.ar: ۞وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِيٓ أَنشَأَ جَنَّٰتࣲ مَّعۡرُوشَٰتࣲ وَغَيۡرَ مَعۡرُوشَٰتࣲ وَٱلنَّخۡلَ وَٱلزَّرۡعَ مُخۡتَلِفًا أُكُلُهُۥ وَٱلزَّيۡتُونَ وَٱلرُّمَّانَ مُتَشَٰبِهࣰ ا وَغَيۡرَ مُتَشَٰبِهࣲۚ كُلُواْ مِن ثَمَرِهِۦٓ إِذَآ أَثۡمَرَ وَءَاتُواْ حَقَّهُۥ يَوۡمَ حَصَادِهِۦۖ وَلَا تُسۡرِفُوٓاْۚ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلۡمُسۡرِفِينَ
6:141.en: He it is Who produceth gardens trellised and untrellised, and the date-palm, and crops of divers flavour, and the olive and the pomegranate, like and unlike. Eat ye of the fruit thereof when it fruiteth, and pay the due thereof upon the harvest day, and be not prodigal. Lo! Allah loveth not the prodigals

49:14.ar: ۞قَالَتِ ٱلۡأَعۡرَابُ ءَامَنَّاۖ قُل لَّمۡ تُؤۡمِنُواْ وَلَٰكِن قُولُوٓاْ أَسۡلَمۡنَا وَلَمَّا يَدۡخُلِ ٱلۡإِيمَٰنُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمۡۖ وَإِن تُطِيعُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ لَا يَلِتۡكُم مِّنۡ أَعۡمَٰلِكُمۡ شَيۡـًٔاۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمٌ
49:14.en: The wandering Arabs say: We believe. Say (unto them, O Muhammad): Ye believe not, but rather say "We submit," for the faith hath not yet entered into your hearts. Yet, if ye obey Allah and His messenger, He will not withhold from you aught of (the reward of) your deeds. Lo! Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

7:179.ar: وَلَقَدۡ ذَرَأۡنَا لِجَهَنَّمَ كَثِيرࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلۡجِنِّ وَٱلۡإِنسِۖ لَهُمۡ قُلُوبࣱ لَّا يَفۡقَهُونَ بِهَا وَلَهُمۡ أَعۡيُنࣱ لَّا يُبۡصِرُونَ بِهَا وَلَهُمۡ ءَاذَانࣱ لَّا يَسۡمَعُونَ بِهَآۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ كَٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِ بَلۡ هُمۡ أَضَلُّۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡغَٰفِلُونَ
7:179.en: Already have We urged unto hell many of the jinn and humankind, having hearts wherewith they understand not, and having eyes wherewith they see not, and having ears wherewith they hear not. These are as the cattle - nay, but they are worse! These are the neglectful

mwKnx6gkOQo.title: Ramadan 2026, Night 7: Quranic Themes 2 - Pillars of Eman
mwKnx6gkOQo.one_line: Three pillars of eman from Al-An'am: listening to Allah's signs, following the prophets as role models, and turning faith into action.
mwKnx6gkOQo.summary: He opens by rejecting 'belief' as a translation of eman: in the West belief means holding something without evidence, while eman is an acknowledgement of Allah built on evidence gathered over a lifetime and lived out through obedience, affirmed in the heart, spoken and acted upon. Al-An'am, focused on the relationship with Allah, gives him three pillars. First, the ability to truly listen: those who respond are those who hear, while people who have killed off their conscience demand miracles they do not need. Animals and birds are nations like us that hear but cannot reflect, and a person who ignores the signs already around him is no better than livestock. Second, role models: no one finds Allah alone, and the long page naming the prophets ends with the command to follow their guidance, as a worshipper follows the imam. Islam came through twenty-three years of the Prophet living the Quran and through chains of people learning from those who learned before them; replacing that with YouTube and AI chatbots, and neglecting scholars, lets knowledge vanish even with books everywhere. Third, action: Allah's gardens are to be eaten and enjoyed, their zakat paid at harvest, and nothing wasted.

outline.heading: Opening
Al-An'am and the relationship with Allah
outline.gist: The surah, reported to have been revealed at once, focuses on the relationship with Allah; its first half defines eman and its second half shows how to practise it.

outline.heading: Eman is not 'belief'
outline.gist: Belief suggests accepting something without evidence; eman is acknowledging Allah from accumulated evidence and committing to Him through obedience, which is why the Bedouins were told to say they had submitted.

outline.heading: Heart, tongue and limbs
outline.gist: Most scholars define eman as affirmation in the heart, verbal declaration and action.

outline.heading: Interlude
Only those who listen respond
outline.gist: You cannot choose what you hear but you choose whether to listen; the 'dead' are those who have killed off their conscience and reason.

outline.heading: Why no miracle?
outline.gist: Allah could send one, but earlier miracles produced no faith and rejecting one brings punishment.

outline.heading: Animals and birds are nations like you
outline.gist: A verse that seems out of place: every creature is a recorded nation that will be gathered to Allah.

outline.heading: First pillar: learning from the signs
outline.gist: Eman requires the ability to hear, reflect and learn from Allah's signs; inherited faith without it is missing pieces.

outline.heading: Hearing without listening
outline.gist: Animals hear but cannot reflect; a person who witnesses without benefiting is no different from them.

outline.heading: Like livestock, or worse
outline.gist: A parallel verse describes people with hearts, eyes and ears they do not use; they are worse than cattle because cattle have no choice.

outline.heading: You don't need a miracle; it's all there
outline.gist: Allah has presented Himself in all of creation; there are those who listen and those who do not.

outline.heading: Beyond survival: guidance depends on listening
outline.gist: Animals reach only survival conclusions while humans can transcend them; Allah guides or leaves astray according to whether one listens.

outline.heading: Interlude
Second pillar: role models
outline.gist: The mind cannot find God alone; growing up sane requires role models, who themselves needed role models, and ours are the prophets.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's argument and Allah's choice
outline.gist: Allah gave Ibrahim his argument and raises in rank whom He wills; questioning His choice of prophets is disrespectful.

outline.heading: Prophets across time with one message
outline.gist: The named prophets came from different eras and places but brought the same message, with the book, judgment and prophethood.

outline.heading: Different outcomes, same steadfastness
outline.gist: Some prophets were killed, expelled, obeyed or ignored; the Prophet is consoled that his people's rejection is not new.

outline.heading: A people who will never reject it
outline.gist: Allah has entrusted the message to others who will carry it, so the Prophet need not be troubled by those who refuse.

outline.heading: 'Follow their guidance': what a role model means
outline.gist: The command means taking them as a model, exactly as one follows the imam in prayer whether one likes him or not.

outline.heading: Islam came through a life, not a book in the desert
outline.gist: The Quran came with twenty-three years of the Prophet living it; without him no one could make sense of it, and we should feel how fortunate we are to have him.

outline.heading: The chain of people learning from people
outline.gist: The companions filled their eyes and ears with the Prophet, the next generations with them, and the Prophet himself learned from earlier prophets.

outline.heading: Learning Islam from YouTube and chatbots
outline.gist: People now take religion from screens and AI rather than from teachers, and the value of scholarship has been downgraded.

outline.heading: Knowledge disappears with the scholars
outline.gist: Allah removes knowledge by taking the scholars, not by erasing books; each scholar who dies without students is a lost link.

outline.heading: Prophets ask for no payment
outline.gist: The prophets sought no wage, only to teach, which is what the message is built on.

outline.heading: Third pillar: eat, pay its due, do not waste
outline.gist: Allah's varied gardens are for eating and enjoying, but zakat is due at harvest and waste is disliked; eman must become behaviour.

themes.label: Eman: faith, certainty, doubt
themes.note: Eman is evidence-based acknowledgement lived through obedience, resting on listening to signs, following role models and acting.

themes.label: Guidance (hidayah)
themes.note: Guidance follows from truly listening to the signs; those who switch off their reason are left in darkness.

themes.label: Knowing Allah / relationship with Allah
themes.note: Allah has presented Himself through His creation, so no further miracle is needed.

themes.label: Stories of earlier prophets
themes.note: The prophets named in Al-An'am are the role models whose guidance believers are commanded to follow.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: The Prophet's lived example is the door through which the Quran is understood.

themes.label: Seeking knowledge, learning and scholars
themes.note: Islam is transmitted through people learning from people; neglecting scholars lets knowledge die.

themes.label: Technology, AI, social media and attention
themes.note: Taking religion from YouTube and AI chatbots replaces the chain of teachers.

themes.label: Zakat, charity and giving
themes.note: Enjoying Allah's provision comes with paying its zakat and not wasting it.
